newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore annual growth forecast cut to 7.1 pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore annual growth forecast cut to 7.1 pct.

text.p: Singapore's economic growth is expected to slow to 7.1 percent this year from 8.8 percent in 1995, a poll of leading financial institutions showed on Wednesday.

All 11 economists polled by Reuters said they had adjusted their year-on-year growth forecasts for 1996 in recent weeks to reflect the impact on the economy of the recent slowdown in the electronics industry, particularly in the United States.
Electronics and related products account for around half Singapore's industrial production and some 60 percent of its non-oil exports.
The analysts had previously predicted an economic growth rate for 1996 of 8.1 percent.

The poll, carried out on Wednesday morning, produced an average forecast for third quarter gross domestic product of 4.9 percent growth year-on-year, compared with 9.8 percent in the third quarter of 1995.
The economy was expected to expand by 6.1 percent in the fourth quarter, compared with 9.1 percent in the last three months of 1995, the poll showed.
"The bottom line is the third quarter will be bad for Singapore manufacturing," said Paul Schymyck, chief regional economist at Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce in Singapore.
"But the economy should pull back up towards the end of the year and overcome its current problems," he added.

Schymyck said Singapore's electronics industry was well entrenched with long-established component suppliers and a good infrastructure which should enable production to rebound once the current slump in electronics orders had ended.
Eddie Lee, economist at Singapore brokerage Vickers Ballas, said all the signs pointed to an improvement in the fourth quarter of the year.
"The fourth quarter will see some kind of bounce," he said.
Singapore's economy expanded by seven percent in the second quarter of 1996 after growing 10.9 percent in the first quarter.
The government has said it expected the economy to grow by between seven and eight percent in 1996.

Economists said monthly data from the U.S. Semiconductor Industry Association had confirmed their fairly bearish view of the electronics sector and the Singapore manufacturing sector in general for the next six months.
The SIA said overnight its so-called book-to-bill ratio, which measures new orders of semiconductors against shipments, had risen to 0.90 in August from a revised 0.86 in July.
A figure below 1.00 in the book-to-bill ratio indicates demand for computer chips is slowing.
The economists said they were heartened by the small rise in the ratio but noted it was still negative and that new orders for U.S. computer chips were down 37.8 percent in August year-on-year.
The U.S. book-to-bill ratio is generally regarded as a key leading indicator for Singapore, with changes in the U.S. data showing up about six months later in the Singapore economy.
"It is just one month's figure," said Yang Sy Jian, research director at RHB-Cathay Securities in Singapore. "We need at least the September figures to confirm the upward trend."
Singapore is expected to publish its official figures for third quarter economic growth in mid-November.
